catalog_quote: This section presents on prosody in Urhobo. I mainly discuss tone here, at both the lexical and grammatical level. ... Tone patterns exist at both the lexical and grammatical level in Urhobo to distinguish linguistic meaning. Tone is correlated with absolute pitch (f0) in Urhobo. Tests have not been taken to determine the degree to which loudness, duration, or phonation play as secondary cues for signaling particular tone categories. ... At the basic level, Urhobo distinguishes between three main tonemes: High, Low, and Downstepped High. Some minimal pairs are found in this dataset showing the role of tone in distinguishing meaning. From the limited number of data I have collected so far, tone is used to distinguish nouns, though not verbs. audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every fragment of the deciding quotation and the dq is verbatim in the held Rolle 2013 text at the stated places (sec. 4/4.1/4.1.1 p.312; sec. 4.2 p.320), and the 'zero occurrences of stress/accent' claim reproduces (grep count 0). (2) The deciding source is a 2013 Berkeley PhonLab working paper from one speaker by an author on first exposure to the language; the specialist literature is Aziza 1997 (PhD, 378 pp) and Aziza 2003 (SAL). (3) Aziza 2003 was fetched sources now (open access) and read: terraced-level tone system, two basic tones plus automatic and non-automatic downstep, tones borne only by vowels, no lexical contour tones, no contrastive length, and no mention of stress or accent anywhere -- it confirms the 'tonal' classification and does not suggest any word stress. sources.citation: Aziza, Rose O. 2003. Tonal alternations in the Urhobo noun phrase. Studies in African Linguistics 32(2): 1-24 [journal pagination]. https://journals.flvc.org/sal/article/download/107341/102662
sources.quote: Abstract: 'The language has two basic tones, high and low, two gliding tones, high-low (falling) and low-high (rising), plus a phenomenon of downstep, both automatic and non-automatic.' p.2: 'The Urhobo tone system has been studied by Kelly (1969), Welmers (1969, 1973), Elugbe (1973, 1989) and Aziza (1997). It has a terraced level tone system with the following characteristics. Only vowels bear tones in this language. There are two basic tones, low (L) and high (H). ... There are no lexical contour tones. ... There is non-automatic downstep (!H) which Welmers regards as a mid tone.' Also p.2:
sources.locator: abstract p.1; section 1 Introduction p.2 (txt lines 17-18, 63-80)
sources.note: Peer-reviewed specialist statement of the Urhobo tone system by the author of the 378-pp tone thesis; our record rests on a 2013 working paper by a first-exposure fieldworker. Confirms 'tonal' and supplies the standard inventory analysis (H, L + non-automatic downstep) to cite alongside Rolle.
